title: Containment and cross-contamination prevention
audience: Supervisors, coordinators and trained cleaners who may be asked to triage, refer or document mould-related work in homes, rentals and commercial buildings, under an approved plan. Not a qualification or authority to remediate, demolish, or certify any building or room.
learningOutcomes: Recognise when containment is required and stop work that lacks it.
Plan a worker and waste route that avoids clean and occupied areas.
Record the zoning and any breach of it.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson
instruction.body: Containment is an approved, supervised measure. This lesson covers recognising the need for it and the planning it requires. It does not authorise a general cleaner to set up or alter containment.

instruction.heading: What the guideline sets for complex work
instruction.body: The WA Department of Health guideline says containment is a core principle of remediation, and that for complex contamination a site-specific remediation plan should be developed with professionals. The plan should cover containment, drying, surface and contents remediation, HVAC work, waste disposal, scheduling, PPE, environmental controls and post-remediation evaluation. The guideline says the affected area must be completely isolated or sealed with heavy grade plastic covers, kept under negative pressure, and that occupants should be evacuated. Those are the guideline's points for complex work, and the approved plan sets how each is done on the job.

instruction.heading: Cross-contamination in practice
instruction.body: Cleaning activity can carry airborne particles into an occupied corridor, so the route through the building must be planned before work starts. Keep clean materials away from the contaminated zone, and keep occupants who are not doing the work outside it. Containment decisions belong to the competent remediation manager. A general cleaner recognises the signs, stops and refers. An experienced remediation manager is needed where containment is complex or occupants are close to the work.

procedure: Identify the zone where work will take place, and the routes past it.
Recognise the need for containment, and stop if the plan does not include it.
Plan the routes for workers, materials and waste before work starts.
Keep occupants who are not part of the work away from the zone.
Confirm that the containment is approved and supervised.
Record the zoning and any breach of it.

workedExamples.situation: Cleaning will take place in a room next to an occupied corridor, and the plan does not show containment.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop before work starts. The plan does not show containment, and the corridor is occupied. Refer to the remediation manager for an approved zoning plan.

workedExamples.situation: A worker carries dusty materials out through the living room to the front door.
workedExamples.reasoning: The route crosses clean and occupied space and carries contamination through them. Stop, record the route and refer for a revised zoning plan.

equipmentAndPpe: Zoning plan approved by the remediation manager.
Barrier tape and signage for the zone boundary.
Training-only sketch of a building. No real containment is set up in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Starting work before the containment is in place.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the containment and zoning in the approved plan before any work begins.

commonErrors.error: Carrying contaminated materials through occupied or clean areas.
commonErrors.prevention: Plan the route before work and use only the approved route.
Refer to the remediation manager. Containment is approved and supervised.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Containment and negative-pressure work are for competent, supervised remediation teams. This lesson does not authorise setting them up.
The containment points come from the WA guideline and apply to buildings in Western Australia.

qualityStandard: The learner recognises when containment is required, and stops work that lacks it.

summary: Plan the routes before work starts.
Keep occupants and clean areas out of the zone.
Refer, and do not set up containment alone.

knowledgeChecks.question: A cleaning job is next to an occupied corridor, and the plan shows no containment. What is correct?
options: Start, because the corridor is only a short distance away.
Stop before work starts and refer for an approved zoning plan.
Start, but close the corridor door.

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the WA guideline say about sealing a complex affected area?
options: It should be sealed with any household tape.
It does not need sealing if the area is small.
It must be completely isolated or sealed with heavy grade plastic covers and kept under negative pressure.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is the route for workers and materials planned before work starts?
options: So that contaminated material does not pass through clean or occupied areas.
So that the crew can finish faster by taking the shortest route.
So that the resident can watch the work.

officialReferences.title: Guidelines for managing mould and dampness: related public health risks in buildings (WA Department of Health)
officialReferences.pageDate: April 2024 (version control table); publication code ENV-0014702 MAY'24; no separate last-updated date shown
officialReferences.covers: Read through a page-summary tool on 2026-11-03 (PDF, Environmental Health Directorate, WA Department of Health). Section 1.4 sets out a general public health duty, a workplace duty and a residential tenancies duty. Section 2.1 names people with existing respiratory, immunocompromising and allergic conditions, and infants, children and older people. Section 3.2.2 says porous items are often not economically salvageable and must be thrown out. Section 3.3 says the source must be located to address the cause and prevent recurrence. Section 3.4.1 defines simple contamination as new, isolated and visible, no greater than one square metre, with easily identified causes, and its footnote calls the one-square-metre size arbitrary. Section 3.4.2 defines complex contamination as larger than one square metre or found in multiple rooms or places. Section 3.5 states there are no defined quantitative or qualitative exposure thresholds for mould or dampness. Section 4.1 lists containment, drying and source repair as principles. Section 4.2.2 advises scrubbing hard surfaces with soapy water, avoiding dry brushing, cleaning at least 30 to 50 cm beyond the visible mould, removing or discarding porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned, stating that mould is not considered hazardous waste, and not painting, sealing or covering surfaces until dry. Section 4.3 recommends a site-specific plan with professionals for complex contamination, isolation with heavy grade plastic and negative pressure, and evacuation of occupants. Section 4.4 lists no recurrence within two to four weeks after remediation as an indicator of success, recommends the evaluation be done by a different entity, and states there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment. Appendix B recommends a P2 or N95 respirator and says PAPRs should be used for complex remediation. Appendix E says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to remediate, demolish, disturb building materials, handle contaminated water or waste, or certify that a building, room or occupant area is safe or free of mould or pathogens. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Restricted or high-exposure remediation is carried out only by an appropriately qualified and competent professional under an approved plan, and some related work, including asbestos and lead disturbance and certain waste handling, is restricted to licensed or specially authorised people. The owner, manager, tenant or contract may define what work is permitted, but where the contract covers only routine cleaning, that is the limit of the task. Where the controlling authority or the competent supervisor is not identified, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: the hazards are unknown or changing; the work is destructive or hazardous and outside the authorised scope; exposure is uncontrolled or the building is unsafe to occupy; supervision, equipment or permissions are insufficient; flood, sewage, asbestos or lead may be present; a worker's PPE or respirator readiness has not been verified; a client asks for a clearance or pathogen-free statement; or a waste route is unauthorised. A stop-work decision is correct. Record it and restart only after the competent supervisor has confirmed the scope in writing.
